en: Abhidhānottaratantra, Chapter 43 [Tibetan & Sanskrit 46] = Lokesh Chandra facsimile edition = 1138 AD palm-leaf manuscript.
Now I shall speak of the commitments (*samaya*) that are difficult to find within the Yoga Tantras:
whether it be a man or a woman, one who proceeds with the conduct of a *siddha*.
It is known that even from afar, those established in their homes or fields [are protected];
the supreme yoga of Heruka is the teacher, the most excellent of yogins. In this tantra, the practitioners are indeed truly virtuous.
They must not be despised, nor should they be reviled; rather, they should be honored with devotion.
For these eight messengers increase devotion and faith;
they are the constant cause of accomplishments and the preservation of the commitments (*samaya*).
For indeed, through the yoga of non-divinity, those who are greedy for desires engage in conceptual constructions;
yet non-duality is unimpeded, characterized by conduct and activity in accordance with the *samaya*.
The practice regarding women, the proper arising, celibacy (*brahmacarya*), and likewise freedom from anger in meditation—[these constitute the path].
Regarding the "transference of wealth," these eight supreme commitments (samayas) must always be known by the practitioner established in the rite;
they are common to all tantras and must not be violated for no reason.
They are grasped by faith alone, not by reason nor by the eye. This secret is unmanifest and must be guarded with great effort.
The wise one, established in the state of the messenger, should move the little finger.
The state of the practitioner is fourfold: pure, impure, mixed, and the state of one who has transcended.
The worshiper is completely purified; the donor is virtuous and free from faults.
The female messengers, possessing the marks of beauty, dwell at the edge of every village.
The messengers [grant] the edge of a sword and the increase of pure merit;
through their excellent association, the practitioner attains accomplishment. Thus, the messengers are accomplished without recitation, meditation, or worship, in a very short time indeed.
Worships proceed, as well as mantras and mudrās together with their wheels.
There is nothing superior to this worship, according to the scripture.
It is for those who have entered the path of the dūtīs and are intent on the welfare of the practitioner.
The practitioner, well-composed and endowed with the knowledge of mantras and spells, should always feed the sacrificial oblation (caru).
One should practice [this] for all castes and should not discriminate regarding food.
Because of the indivisibility of reality (*tattva*), there are two female messengers (*dūtī*) in the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).
In the case of the movement of the intellect (*dhī*), there is only one messenger.
Having been awakened, one should not transgress what has been consecrated;
desiring one's own welfare and desiring that [welfare], one should bring about happiness together with these [three], having performed the conduct of the samaya.
With that very [practice], the "whirling of the ground" is described:
at night one should always remain naked, and one's clothing should always be black or red;
for the sake of happiness, one should move about comfortably, clothed in garments made from the limbs of living beings.
Having completely cast off the sacred thread (*yajñopavīta*), one abides in Śrī Heruka through purification; bound by the five mudrās, one remains constantly established [in that state].
Free from the obstruction of pleasure, with the casting away of the faces of *cal* and *calla*.
First, purity through the messenger (dūtī) is desired; second, purity through yoga is intended; sitting together in one place and the sacrificial oblation (caru) are said to be the third purity.
From the maintenance of these purities, one attains purification in due order.
Having attained [this], for whom would success not arise?
As it is stated in the *Tattvasaṃgraha*, so too it is stated in the *Cakrasaṃvara*;
it is fully proclaimed in the *Guhyatantra* and likewise in the *Haritantra*.
In the Mahābhairava [tantra], the practitioner of mantra accomplishes the granting of success for recitation, vows, and so forth by mere meditation in an instant;
he should undertake this purification for those devoted to the path of yoga.
The merit of those who are pure cannot be told by a single mouth; the expansion of virtues in a practitioner cannot be expressed even by hundreds of thousands of mouths.
The wisdom of Śrī Heruka is pure, the means for accomplishing all characteristics;
through drinking the water of bliss, it is meritorious, purifying, and the destroyer of evil—
for the best of men who practices it through touch or even through meditation.
With a self purified of all evil, one attains the glory of the Tathāgatas;
in birth after birth, one is born into the family of the Tathāgatas,
and becomes either a universal monarch (cakravartin) or a sovereign of the world.
Having thus always performed worship, one should offer oblations with devotion.

Having worshipped the Excellent One (Vara) and Viśuddhi, one should likewise worship the Hero who has emerged from Nirvāṇa; by that, one’s own self is worshipped, as well as the entire world of the moving and the unmoving.
One should worship the host of brothers and daughters-in-law, established in the union with Soma.

Among the three-and-a-half brothers, one should not reveal the arising of pleasure or pain, nor the knowledge (*jñāna*), the mantra, or the mudrā. One should consume the four [substances], and thus one becomes one who has performed the conduct of the pure samaya.
One should not give the mantra to anyone, nor should one destroy the instruction;
however, one should give the instruction according to the truth to those who abide by the samaya.
Bewildered by the Krama, one should not go to any other woman except for the dūtī.

The messenger (dūtī) is said to always grant liberation; one should offer her food even by transgressing [ordinary rules]. One should not show [worldly] honor to those well-established [in the path], even if they are of low birth.
Indeed, mother, sister, daughter, and wife are all established as messengers.
Wherein his effort is diminished, there likewise is the success of the wheel;
one should attract the supreme, for this is the certain rule regarding the substance. The yogi, always practicing the left-hand way (vāmācāra), should step forward with the left foot first.
Turning with the left hand, honoring the left half [of the body],
with the left side of the body concealed, and consuming the offerings made with the left; such a practitioner,
who does not violate his vows and fulfills them, is devoted to the *samaya*.
According to the conduct of the *samaya*-family, there is the eating of the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) together in one place;
this is the practice of the outer mandala for the four castes [... [141 deest] [...
the uniform practice that fulfills the accomplishment of yoga.
One should prepare a triangular maṇḍala for the mantrins using beef, horse meat, and dog meat.
Even a Buddha certainly perishes.
This heroic feast for heroes is endowed with both mudrās and mantras.
Likewise, the emanation of Śrī Heruka is distinguished by the treatises on ritual service.
One should constantly perform the retention [of the mantra] and provide protection for all activities so that they may be accomplished without obstacle; no one else attains success in this way.
His messenger is excellent.
And she is the goddess who is intent upon the great purpose.
Unattached due to the enjoyment of passion, she is manifested through the substances of yoga.
She is intensely devoted to the instructions of the guru and is equal to the essence of wealth.
O Lord, in an instant he beholds his brother or even his father.
She has a thick tongue, tawny eyes, a dark complexion, and tawny hair.
It is the common practice for all practitioners, always devoted to recitation and vows;
it is joined with the syllable *smaraṇa* and endowed with words such as *dūbhya*.
The twenty-four heroic ḍākinīs bestow the fruits of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.
This heart-mantra is victorious at all times and accomplishes all desired aims.
It bestows the fruit of the play of yoga.
Mantras arise spontaneously within the three worlds, including all things mobile and immobile.
For embodied beings, the presence of the mantra does not arise if it is devoid of the mudrās that are conjoined with the mantra and mudrās.
It is to be understood through the Atiyoga; those who, due to their lack of heat (*uṣman*) and so forth, harbor hatred toward Mahāyoga—which accomplishes all desires and goals—[are lost].
Having gone to his own womb, he is even born among the Caṇḍālas.
Just as someone seeking ghee obtains it easily through faith, so too [is this].
But ghee is not produced; there is only the affliction of the body.
Otherwise, O Lord, your breaking of the fast and your worship would be in vain.
Because they are the cause for the means of livelihood, they are based on association with others.
In whatever land the heroes who uphold the great yoga dwell, [there success is found].
Even a Caṇḍāla, a Mleccha, or a Dhūrtaka may consider that region to be their own domain.
I always abide within it for the sake of gathering sentient beings.
[In the Abhidhānottara, in the chapter on the Bliss of the Messenger and the Waters, the thirty-fourth.
